title: Road safety statistics for 2025 confirm drop in EU road deaths
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: Today, the European Commission released the final figures on road fatalities for 2025, reporting 19,350 deaths due to road crashes. This represents a 3% decrease from 2024 and a 15% decrease from 2019, equivalent to 580 fewer deaths on European roads compared to 2024, and 3,400 fewer deaths compared to 2019. While this significant achievement reaffirms the EU's position as one of the world's safest regions for road travel, the majority of Member States are not yet on track to meet the EU target of halving road deaths and serious injuries by 2030. Results confirm that only five countries are on course to meet the 50% reduction target in road deaths by 2030: Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, Poland and Romania. Despite their progress since 2019, Bulgaria and Romania, alongside Croatia, continue to have the highest fatality rates in the EU when measuring deaths per million inhabitants (71, 68 and 65 deaths per million). On the opposite end of the ranking, Sweden and Denmark report the lowest fatality rates, with 19 and 24 deaths per million inhabitants respectively. Based on the reported data, elderly people are more often victims of road crashes than other age groups, while passenger cars and vulnerable road users such as pedestrians, cyclists and motorcycle users and are the most exposed to road casualties. Finally, most road deaths happen in rural roads outside urban areas. For every road fatality, an estimated five people are seriously injured. This means that around 100 thousand people across the EU suffer serious injuries in road crashes each year, with serious implications on physical, psychological, and socioeconomic wellbeing for the victims and their families. The figures published today reveal the final numbers of road fatalities for 2025, following the publication of preliminary data in March 2026. Apostolos Tzitzikostas, European Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism, said: "Road safety is about more than rules and regulations. It is about protecting lives and preventing tragedies that affect families and communities across Europe. In the European Union, every life lost on our roads is one too many. Our goal is clear: to ensure that every citizen, wherever they travel and whatever their mode of transport, can reach their destination. This means making our roads safer, strengthening prevention and ensuring that every journey ends safely." Estimates for the first half of 2026 Provisional data shows that the number of countries reporting a reduction of fatalities above 5% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025 is higher than those which report increases in road deaths, hinting a positive signal for the EU in reducing road fatalities in 2026. These provisional figures should, however, be interpreted with caution. In some countries, due to small numbers, these figures are subject to significant year-on-year fluctuations. Furthermore, road fatalities are subject to seasonality, with higher incidence of crashes over the summer period. The European Commission will continue to monitor these trends closely and support Member States in addressing emerging concerns. EU Road safety conference 2026 The 2026 EU Road Safety Conference will take place on 23 November 2026, at the Charlemagne Building in Brussels. This flagship event marks the halfway point in Europe’s 10-year strategy to halve road deaths and serious injuries by 2030 and will bring together policymakers, researchers, civil society leaders, and the private sector to explore the future of safe road transport in the EU. Discussion will focus on critical emerging issues, such as the use of health data for road safety, the rise of connected and automated vehicles, as well as the growing importance of data driven policy and decision making. During the event, the Commission will also announce the winners of the 2026 Excellence in Road Safety Awards, celebrating the continent’s most inspiring and impactful road safety initiatives. Background In 2018, the EU set itself a 50% reduction target for road deaths and serious injuries by 2030, while aiming to reach close to zero road deaths by 2050 (‘Vision Zero’). The Commission published a report on the Implementation of the EU Road Safety Policy Framework at the Mid-Point in 2026. The report confirms that significant progress has been made in reducing road fatalities, but the current pace is still insufficient. Road safety is a shared responsibility between the EU and Member States. While national and local authorities carry out most of the day-to-day work, the EU contributes with safety rules for infrastructure and vehicles and for driving testing and licencing, coordinates cross-border cooperation between authorities and efforts to exchange best practices, and funds road safety projects. Recent EU-level initiatives include updated requirements for driving licences and better cross-border enforcement of road traffic rules and a proposal to enhance the roadworthiness of vehicles. Today’s figures are based on final data for 2025 submitted to the Commission by EU Member States for the CARE database of Road Accidents in the EU, and from national sources otherwise, some of them still provisional and subject to possible revisions. The preliminary statistics for the full year 2026 will be published in March 2027. title: Powering jobs: Employment under the EU’s passenger car CO2 standards - International Council on Clean Transportation
source_name: 国际清洁交通委员会 ICCT
content: Report Powering jobs: Employment under the EU’s passenger car CO2 standards Overview The EU passenger car sector is undergoing a profound transformation as it transitions from internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) to battery electric vehicles (BEVs). Some studies have projected substantial job losses in passenger car production in Europe due to this transition, with industry stakeholders arguing that the EU vehicle carbon dioxide (CO2) standards could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk. This study assesses employment outcomes under three alternative CO2 regulatory pathways across passenger car production, battery production and recycling, and charging infrastructure, covering EU-produced vehicles for both EU and export markets. Weighing job losses in combustion engine vehicle production against employment gains across emerging industries, it shows how employment may shift during the transition. Key findings By 2035, employment in EU car production, battery production and recycling, and charging infrastructure is projected to grow modestly (+2%) if current CO2 standards are maintained, grow further (+10%) if measures are introduced that strengthen EU-based production of battery electric vehicles and related supply chains, and decline (−6%) if standards are delayed or weakened. The analysis finds that under the Current Standards (baseline) scenario, which reflects the EU’s existing CO2 standards and a requirement that every new car sold in 2035 is a BEV, total employment in the EU across car production would remain broadly stable (2% above 2025 levels). Here, growth in BEV production and related industries—including battery production and recycling and charging infrastructure—would offset job losses from declining ICEV production in the long term. Under the Policy Action scenario, which combines current CO2 standards with measures to strengthen EU production of BEVs and related industries, employment is projected to increase by 10% between 2025 and 2035. Under the Delayed Standards scenario, which assumes a 5-year delay in the implementation of the CO2 standards, employment is projected to decrease by 6% between 2025 and 2035. Employment differences between scenarios are driven by the combined effects of the powertrain mix and the share of vehicles produced in the EU. Although we estimate BEV production to require around 30% fewer jobs per vehicle than ICEV production, the transition would still yield higher long-term employment as a result of higher EU production shares combined with growth in battery production, recycling, and charging infrastructure. To a lesser extent, differences in EU production for non-EU markets contribute further to this gap. Employment differences between scenarios are most visible at the Member State level, because passenger car production is concentrated in a small number of countries. Compared with maintaining the current regulation, delaying the implementation of the CO2 standards for passenger cars is projected to reduce jobs in all EU Member States in 2035. The largest impacts are projected for Germany, the EU’s largest car producer, followed by the EU’s other top producers of passenger cars, including France, Poland, Italy, and Spain. Although a delayed transition to BEVs would temporarily preserve jobs in ICEV-related activities, it would also reduce employment growth in BEV production and related industries in the long term, ultimately leading to substantial job losses. Policy recommendations The findings suggest that the most effective way to avoid job losses and instead support job gains in the passenger car sector is to maintain the current CO2standards and complement them with industrial policies that enable the EU to capture a growing share of jobs in BEV production and related battery and charging infrastructure industries. This would also provide regulatory predictability and investment certainty across BEV production and emerging industries. Accordingly, driving job growth amid the transition to BEVs requires: - Maintaining the current CO2 standards trajectory, including the 2035 and intermediate 2030 targets. We project that both the 2030 and 2035 CO2 targets for cars will support long-term employment across vehicle production and BEV-related industries such as battery production and recycling and charging infrastructure related jobs. Although delaying the transition to BEVs may support ICEV production in the short term, it reduces job growth in BEV production and related industries, yielding lower overall employment in the long term. - Complementing the current CO2 standards with industrial incentives to enhance EU BEV production. The analysis estimates that job creation is highest when EU-based manufacturers produce a larger share of BEVs sold in and exported from the EU. To capture this potential, the CO2 standards could be complemented by measures that increase the EU’s domestic manufacturing base across BEV, battery, and charging infrastructure supply chains. Policy scenarios Three policy scenarios are considered: - The Current Standards (baseline) scenario reflected the CO2 standards adopted in June 2025, including the fleet averaging mechanism for 2025–2027 (Regulation [EU] 2025/1214). Under this pathway, manufacturers must reduce average tailpipe CO2 by 55% by 2030 (relative to 2021 levels) and reach 100% zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) in new passenger car sales by 2035. - The Policy Action scenario preserved the 2030 and 2035 targets but assumed additional measures to strengthen EU value creation, such as local content policies (including measures proposed at the EU level under the Industry Accelerator Act [European Commission, 2026b] and national-level approaches) and targeted production incentives (e.g., subsidies for the production of vehicles and batteries). Rather than modeling these measures individually in the analysis, we incorporated broad assumptions linking them to a higher EU production share of BEVs and PHEVs. - The Delayed Standards scenario assumed a 5-year delay in the implementation of the CO2 standards. As a result, electrification would progress more slowly, with BEV and PHEV shares increasing moderately through 2030 before reaching 100% BEVs in 2040. This 5-year delay was a simplifying assumption: in practice, a weakening of the regulation could take various forms, including additional credits for BEVs and PHEVs, averaging mechanisms, or other compliance flexibilities.
